articles.title: How to Test AI Provider Timeouts Before Production
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance. When an application depends on an AI provider, write down what your app should do when the provider times out before you wire up retries. Other…
articles.body: Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance. When an application depends on an AI provider, write down what your app should do when the provider times out before you wire up retries. Otherwise, a slow request can tie up a worker and a retry can accidentally start the same job twice. Give the request a deadline Start with the time a user can reasonably wait for the feature. If a page has a five-second budget, the model call needs a shorter deadline so the app has time to return a useful response. If the work routinely takes longer, give the user a job ID and show its status instead of holding the page open. Test the failure paths without calling the provider Use a stub provider in your test environment.

articles.title: Read Your Own Writes on Async Replicas: PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN
articles.excerpt: PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN lets a read on an asynchronous replica wait until that replica has replayed your write. You get read-your-writes consistency without sending every read to the primary. Rea…
articles.body: PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN lets a read on an asynchronous replica wait until that replica has replayed your write. You get read-your-writes consistency without sending every read to the primary. The problem: the write succeeded, the read missed it Read-write splitting is a common way to scale: writes go to the primary, reads spread across asynchronous replicas. It breaks a simple expectation: A user renames their profile from Alex to Sam. The primary commits. Success. The user refreshes, and the read lands on a replica. The replica hasn't replayed the change yet, so it returns Alex. Nothing failed. Replication lag let the user miss their own write. The guarantee that this never happens is called read-your-writes (RYW) consistency . Why not just read from the primary?

articles.body: Moving a cursor with only your thoughts just cleared a historic FDA hurdle. The fine print matters just as much as the headline. On November 25, 2026, Neuralink announced FDA approval to launch the LINK Pivotal Study. The company described it as the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the United States — a U.S. first for this kind of brain-implant study. The trial will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the system in people with severe paralysis due to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). That includes whether participants can control digital devices through thought and gain independence in daily life, plus long-term safety and reliability across multiple clinical sites. Enrollment is now open.

articles.title: Treat printed QR destinations as a web release contract
articles.excerpt: A QR code on a card can outlive the landing page it points to. Once the card is printed, changing a route in the CMS does not update the destination in anyone’s pocket. Treat that encoded URL as a sma…
articles.body: A QR code on a card can outlive the landing page it points to. Once the card is printed, changing a route in the CMS does not update the destination in anyone’s pocket. Treat that encoded URL as a small public interface, not incidental artwork. Record the contract before printing For each print run, record the exact decoded URL, its intended final destination, a named owner and the point at which the link can be retired. Use an HTTPS URL a team can maintain. Keep the encoded path independent of campaign copy or a CMS slug likely to change. Print a short human-readable address too, so the journey is not scan-only. For example, a synthetic stall might print https://example.com/card and send it to /collections/weekend . Before changing the collection’s slug, test the printed URL itself.

articles.body: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR We got Samsung’s private AI cloud, referred to as “SPAC” in the code, working with AI select on a Galaxy S26 Ultra running One UI 9.5 Beta 1, producing more accurate calendar event extraction than its standard processing. Code references show SPAC supports Google’s Gemma 4 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 (used in our test) and appears to route encrypted requests through a third-party relay to hide user identity. articles.title: 'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'
articles.excerpt: Colorful metaphors, a near-miss with Eddie Murphy and humpback whales in 20th-century California.
articles.body: It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp? Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.
